[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Understanding NumPy ndarray Architecture and Memory Layout"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"The core of NumPy's high performance is the ndarray object. Unlike standard Python lists, which are arrays of pointers scattered across memory, a NumPy ndarray is a contiguous block of homogeneous data coupled with a metadata descriptor known as the strided-memory view."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Anatomy of an ndarray"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Under the hood, a NumPy array is structured as a C struct that points to a block of memory. It consists primarily of a data pointer (pointing to the first byte of the array), data type information (dtype), shape (dimensions), and strides (the number of bytes to step in each dimension)."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"import numpy as np

arr = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]], dtype=np.int64)
print("Shape:", arr.shape)
print("Strides:", arr.strides)
print("Element size (bytes):", arr.itemsize)"},{"order":6,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding Strides"},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"Strides are crucial for understanding how NumPy traverses memory. A stride tells NumPy how many bytes it must skip in memory to move to the next position along a given axis."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"For a 64-bit integer array (8 bytes per element) with shape (2, 3), the strides are typically (24, 8)."},{"order":9,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Moving along axis 0 (rows) requires skipping 24 bytes (3 elements * 8 bytes)."},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Moving along axis 1 (columns) requires skipping 8 bytes (1 element * 8 bytes)."},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"C-Contiguous vs. Fortran-Contiguous Layouts"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"Memory layout determines the order in which multi-dimensional arrays are stored linearly in computer memory."},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"C-contiguous (Row-major): The last index changes the fastest. This is the default in NumPy."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Fortran-contiguous (Column-major): The first index changes the fastest. This is common in MATLAB and older Fortran libraries."},{"order":15,"type":"code","text":"c_arr = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]], order='C')
f_arr = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]], order='F')

print("Is C-contiguous:", c_arr.flags['C_CONTIGUOUS'])
print("Is F-contiguous:", f_arr.flags['F_CONTIGUOUS'])"},{"order":16,"type":"subheading","text":"Performance Implications"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"Cache locality dictates execution speed in modern CPUs. Accessing memory in a stride-aligned, contiguous manner minimizes cache misses, enabling vectorized operations via SIMD instructions. Writing code that respects the underlying memory layout leads to significant speedups in heavy numerical computations."}]
